title: 5 Strategies To Avoid With Difficult Students oid-with-difficult-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies five commonly recommended but ultimately ineffective strategies for handling difficult students: behavior contracts, ignoring misbehavior, recess time-out supervised by non-classroom staff, permanent seating separation, and special rewards or praise tied to ordinary expected behavior. He explains why each produces only short-term improvement while causing longer-term harm, such as labeling students, weakening intrinsic motivation, or communicating that a student is fundamentally different from peers. He closes by arguing that most difficult students improve fastest when subjected to the exact same classroom management plan as everyone else, since being treated as an equal — rather than singled out — is what allows them to change.
points: Behavior contracts produce fast but short-lived improvement while labeling students and undermining intrinsic motivation over time.
Ignoring difficult students' misbehavior usually backfires, often escalating attention-getting behavior rather than reducing it.
Recess time-out only works if supervised by the student's own classroom teacher; otherwise it functions as a weak, meaningless consequence.
Permanent seating separation ('permanent time-out') is described as another form of labeling that signals the teacher has given up on the student.
Difficult students make the most lasting progress when held to the exact same classroom management plan as every other student in the class.
quotes: Any strategy that involves a “do this and get that” scenario weakens over time and does nothing to spark intrinsic motivation—which is the one ingredient necessary for real, lasting improvement.
Most of the time the student being ignored will respond by ratcheting up his or her attention-getting behavior, at times going so far as to sing, yell, or even laugh while you’re trying to teach.

Recess time-out only works if you, as the classroom teacher, are the one doing the supervising. Otherwise, it’s a weak consequence, sitting there with a whole band of troublemakers from all over the school.
Permanent time-out merely reinforces in the student’s mind that he or she is a behavior problem. It becomes part of who they are, like their eye color or where they were born.
Most difficult students are able to make lasting changes in behavior when they’re subject to the same solid classroom management plan as everybody else.
